title: Batch vs Streaming — Choosing an Approach
summary: A decision framework for when a pipeline should be batch, micro-batch, or streaming — driven by the actual latency requirement, not by which architecture sounds most impressive.

slides.markdown:
"Should this be batch or streaming?" is one of the most common architecture questions in a data engineering interview, and the strong answer always starts from one number: **how fresh does the data actually need to be, in business terms?**

Batch, micro-batch, and streaming aren't a maturity ladder where streaming is the "advanced" version of batch — they're three points on a latency/cost/complexity curve, and picking the wrong one either wastes engineering effort on freshness nobody asked for, or ships a dashboard too stale to be useful.

This topic gives you the filter to answer that question fast, and the discipline to resist building streaming because it's the more exciting build.

slides.sectionTitle: Latency requirement as the first filter
slides.markdown:
Before anything else, ask: **what happens if this data is an hour late? A minute late? Ten seconds late?**

- If the honest answer is "nothing bad happens, it's a daily report someone checks each morning" — you need batch, and building anything more sophisticated is wasted effort.
- If the answer is "a fraud transaction clears before we can flag it" or "a user sees a stale cart total" — you need something close to real time.

This single question does more filtering work than any architecture diagram, because it forces a concrete business consequence onto the table before a single tool gets chosen. Most "we need real-time" requests, pressed on this question, turn out to tolerate minutes just fine.

slides.sectionTitle: Batch vs micro-batch vs continuous streaming
slides.markdown:
| | Batch | Micro-batch | Continuous streaming |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Typical latency** | Hours | Seconds to minutes | Sub-second to seconds |
| **Processing unit** | Large scheduled chunk | Small scheduled chunk, frequent | Individual event or tiny window |
| **Infra** | Cron/orchestrator + batch compute | Same tooling, tighter schedule, or Spark Structured Streaming | Kafka/Flink/Kinesis-style stream processor |
| **Operational cost** | Lowest | Moderate | Highest — always-on infra, harder failure recovery |
| **Typical use** | Nightly warehouse loads, BI dashboards | "Real-time-ish" dashboards, near-real-time ETL | Fraud detection, live pricing, alerting |

The honest fact most vendors don't advertise: continuous streaming's operational cost — always-on consumers, backpressure handling, exactly-once delivery semantics — is substantially higher than either batch alternative, which is exactly why it should be reserved for cases that truly need it.

slides.sectionTitle: Cost and complexity scale with realtime-ness
slides.markdown:
Each step toward lower latency adds real, ongoing engineering cost, not just a different scheduling interval:

- **Batch** fails safe — if a nightly job errors, you retry it tomorrow (or today) with no data loss, and the blast radius is one late dashboard.
- **Streaming** has to handle failures *while data keeps arriving*: a consumer crash mid-stream needs exactly the right offset-tracking to avoid dropping or duplicating events, backpressure has to be handled when downstream can't keep up, and state (for windowed aggregations) has to be checkpointed and recovered correctly.

That added complexity is a permanent tax paid by every future engineer who touches the system, not a one-time build cost — a streaming pipeline needs an on-call rotation that understands consumer lag and rebalancing, which is a genuinely different skill set than debugging a failed cron job.

Here's the thing most "real-time" pipelines actually are: **micro-batch**, not continuous streaming. A job that runs every 1-5 minutes, reading whatever landed since the last run, delivers freshness that feels real-time to a human looking at a dashboard, while keeping the operational model of batch — a job runs, finishes, and either succeeded or failed cleanly.

Spark Structured Streaming's default trigger mode is literally micro-batch under the hood, even though it's marketed as "streaming" — because for the vast majority of use cases, sub-minute freshness with batch-style failure semantics beats sub-second freshness with streaming-style operational complexity.

The honest recommendation for most teams evaluating "batch vs streaming": try micro-batch first. Reach for continuous, event-by-event streaming only when you've confirmed the latency requirement genuinely can't tolerate even a one-minute window.

slides.sectionTitle: Building streaming because it sounds impressive
slides.markdown:
The recurring failure mode: a team builds a Kafka-based streaming pipeline for a use case that batch would have served just fine, because streaming is the more exciting thing to put on a resume or pitch to leadership — not because the latency requirement demanded it.

The cost shows up later, not immediately: six months in, the team is debugging consumer group rebalancing at 1am for a dashboard that genuinely only needed to refresh nightly, and nobody on the team had operated a streaming system before this one. The business got zero additional value from the lower latency — nobody was making decisions faster because the data was 30 seconds old instead of 6 hours old — but the team pays the operational cost indefinitely.

The check that prevents this: before building streaming, name the specific decision or action that becomes possible with lower latency, and confirm someone will actually act on it within that window. If the answer is "nobody's workflow changes," the latency doesn't matter yet.

In order, the questions that actually decide this:

1. **Freshness SLA** — what's the maximum acceptable staleness, defined by a real consequence, not a vibe?
2. **Data volume and velocity** — is it a firehose that streaming tooling is built for, or a moderate volume that a scheduled job handles fine?
3. **Downstream consumer needs** — does the consumer (a dashboard, a model, an alert) actually change behavior based on freshness, or is it read once a day regardless?
4. **Team's operational maturity** — does the team have (or can it afford to build) the on-call and debugging skill set streaming infrastructure demands?

If question 1 doesn't demand sub-minute freshness, stop there — batch or micro-batch wins on cost and simplicity, and questions 2-4 barely matter.

The same use case makes the trade-off concrete when you compare both real implementations side by side.

![Fraud detection compared: nightly batch scoring versus real-time streaming scoring](assets/fraud-batch-vs-stream.svg)

Batch loses here for a structural reason, not a performance one: by the time a nightly job flags a fraudulent transaction, the money is already gone. This is the canonical case where the business consequence of latency is unambiguous and severe enough to justify streaming's operational cost.

slides.markdown:
The one-line version of this whole topic: **default to batch or micro-batch, and justify streaming with a specific, named business consequence of latency — not with "real-time is better."**

The rest of this curriculum's Batch Processing group goes deep on the batch side — extraction patterns, CDC, orchestration, idempotency — because that's where most data engineering work actually lives. A later Stream Processing group covers the streaming side with the same depth once you've confirmed you actually need it.

Interviewers ask this question specifically to see whether a candidate reaches for complexity by reflex or by requirement — the checklist from this topic is the fast, defensible way to show the latter.
